nodes.label: The Science Wars, 1994–2000
nodes.date_label: Higher Superstition 1994 · Social Text "Science Wars" issue and Sokal's hoax 1996 · The Golem in Physics Today 1996–97 · Impostures intellectuelles 1997 (English 1998) · A House Built on Sand 1998 · Pandora's Hope and Shapin's reply 1999 · Later reading: Latour 2004
nodes.description: A dispute of the mid-1990s in which scientists and philosophers charged science studies with relativism and hostility to science, and sociologists and historians of science answered them. It is taught here as a moment in the reception of science studies: most of the attackers were scientists or philosophers, not historians. Gross and Levitt's Higher Superstition (1994) went after what an SHPS editorial called the "exponents of science studies -- that is, historians, philosophers and sociologists of science", the Edinburgh strong programme among them. Social Text planned a "Science Wars" issue in response; Sokal's parody appeared in it (1996), and his confession attacked "epistemic relativism" in cultural studies. In Physics Today Mermin judged that The Golem showed "what can go wrong if you focus too strongly on the social perspective", and Collins and Pinch replied that many scientists were "scientific fundamentalists". Sokal and Bricmont (1997; English 1998) called the strong programme "either a valid and mildly interesting corrective ... or else a gross and blatant error" and charged Latour with sliding from "Nature's representation" to "Nature". Historians of science answered: Shapin (1999) called the charge of hostility to science "malevolently misinformed", and Latour wrote that science studies had "added reality to science, not withdrawn any from it" (1999).

nodes.scope_note: A debate entry about the reception of science studies, measured through its texts. The texts read are listed in the source notes; several central ones were not. Higher Superstition was not read: its words are given only as its in-period readers (Edge, Jardine and Frasca-Spada, Sokal and Bricmont) quote them. Wise's Isis review, the Social Text essays, Latour's Le Monde article of 18 January 1997, most of A House Built on Sand (read only in publisher abstracts), Kitcher's and Hacking's books and The Golem itself were not read. The Jardine and Frasca-Spada editorial is the only source for Latour's Le Monde wording; the same journal later printed an "Apology" by the two editors (1997, unread), so that wording should be checked before it is relied on. Pandora's Hope was read in a retyped copy without book pages. Sokal's 1996 confession named no sociologist of science; his criticism of SSK and Latour dates from 1997. Mermin was a qualified critic who later defended Latour. Jardine and Frasca-Spada criticised both sides and are not drawn as one-way critics. Hacking and Kitcher present themselves as mediators and are not drawn as critics. Haraway and Latour are treated as broadly aligned (editorial decision, 2026-10-14); Haraway is not drawn as a critic of Latour. The 2000 end of the label is a convenience: Latour's 2004 retrospective is cited as a dated later reading, and later collections (The One Culture?, 2001; After the Science Wars, 2001) are named but unread.

strands.title: Higher Superstition and its first answers, 1994–97
strands.focus: Gross and Levitt attacked the academic left's views of science, including "exponents of science studies" and the Edinburgh strong programme; Wise in Isis and Edge from Edinburgh answered them. The book is known here only through its readers, so its targets are given as they reported them.

edges.relationship: Scientists and philosophers charge that the strong programme and The Golem leave nature out of the explanation of scientific belief (1994–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal, "What the Social Text Affair Does and Does Not Prove" (author's text, 1997; printed 1998; cited by note): "The extreme versions of social constructivism and relativism -- such as the Edinburgh 'strong programme' -- are, I think, largely based on the same failure to distinguish clearly between ontology, epistemology, and the sociology of knowledge"; he quotes Collins (n. 10) as saying "the natural world has a small or non-existent role in the construction of scientific knowledge", while allowing that Collins may intend a methodological injunction. Sokal and Bricmont, Intellectual Impostures (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing): most scientists "point out the substantial missing piece in this kind of explanation: Nature itself" (p. 79); the strong programme "is ambiguous in its intent; and, depending on how one resolves the ambiguity, it becomes either a valid and mildly interesting corrective to the most naive psychological and sociological notions - reminding us that 'true beliefs have causes too' - or else a gross and blatant error" (p. 84). Mermin, Physics Today 49:3 (1996), p. 11: Collins and Pinch "infer from these studies a seriously deficient picture of the scientific enterprise"; The Golem is "an instructive demonstration of what can go wrong if you focus too strongly on the social perspective". Mermin frames this as a question of balance, not a refutation. Gross and Levitt (1994; book unread) are known here only through Edge (1997, n. 4), who reports that they name "the 'strong programme' in sociology of science associated with the Edinburgh school" (p. 25) and Bloor (p. 52) while listing no work by Barnes or Bloor in their references. The replies are the separate ssk → sciencewars edge. Two targets share this arrow: the Edinburgh strong programme (Barnes, Bloor, Henry), named by Gross and Levitt (as quoted), Sokal, and Sokal and Bricmont; and The Golem of Collins and Pinch, Mermin's target, which belongs with SSK's replication studies. No strand is set for that reason.
edges.map_label: Strong programme and The Golem attacked, 1994–98

edges.relationship: Sociologists of scientific knowledge answer that their methodological relativism was misread as hostility to science (1996–97)
edges.evidence_note: In-period replies in the sociologists' own words. Collins and Pinch, letter in Physics Today 49:7 (1996), p. 11, answering Mermin: "Many scientists, especially those who have become spokespersons, are evidently scientific fundamentalists. ... Where we sociologists think of ourselves as trying to gain social and historical insight into science, the fundamentalists see heresy"; The Golem is "about as inoffensive a social analysis of science as one could wish for"; they cite historical work on the slow reception of relativity. Mermin replied on the same page that "the rightness/wrongness axis is not a relevant dimension in their kind of sociological analysis of science". David Edge, "The Umpire Strikes Back" (EASST web text, February 1997; read in a web reproduction): "A powerful group of American scientists, apparently for political reasons, have chosen to mount a vicious attack on those scholars whom they take to be 'flying from science and reason'. One of their prime targets is 'social constructivism'"; the Edinburgh group "has always maintained that reality plays a central role in what comes to be believed about it". Edge is not on the ssk roster; he is on this debate's roster. Shapin's 1999 defence of methodological relativism is carried by the science → sciencewars edge. Bloor's own reply to the warriors was not found; his 1999 complaint that Latour joined "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" is on the ssk → latour edge.

edges.relationship: Physicists charge Latour with sliding from representations of nature to nature and with misreading relativity (1996–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal and Bricmont, Intellectual Impostures (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing): Latour's works "contain a great number of propositions formulated so ambiguously that they can hardly be taken literally" (p. 85); on the Third Rule of Method, "Note how Latour slips, without comment or argument, from 'Nature's representation' in the first half of this sentence to 'Nature' tout court in the second half" (p. 85); his 1988 article on relativity "illustrates perfectly the problems encountered by a sociologist who aims to analyse the content of a scientific theory he does not understand very well" (p. 115), and "Latour's analysis is fatally flawed by his inadequate understanding of the theory Einstein is trying to explain" (p. 121). Sokal (1997/98, cited by note): "Latour has produced 40 pages of comical misunderstandings of a theory that is nowadays routinely taught to intelligent college freshmen"; Sokal in Le Monde (31 January 1997, author's translation): Latour "mixes up ontology and epistemology, and he attacks positions that no one would defend". Weinberg (New York Review of Books, 1996): "The objective nature of scientific knowledge has been denied by Andrew Ross and Bruno Latour". Dissent among physicists: Mermin (Physics Today 50:10, 1997, p. 11) wrote of the relativity essay, "I believe such attacks miss the point of Latour's essay". Steve Fuller's report of the Sokal–Latour debate at the LSE (1998) judged that "Latour won 'on points'". Latour's replies are the separate latour → sciencewars edge.

edges.relationship: Latour answers the physicists: science studies "added reality to science" and is "not at war" (1996–99)
edges.evidence_note: His own words where read. Pandora's Hope (1999), ch. 1, "Do You Believe in Reality? News from the Trenches of the Science Wars" (read in a retyped copy without book pages; to be checked against the printed book): "in this guerrilla warfare being conducted in the no-man's-land between the 'two cultures,' we were the ones being attacked by militants, activists, sociologists, philosophers, and technophobes of all hues, precisely because of our interest in the inner workings of scientific facts"; "If science studies has achieved anything, I thought, surely it has added reality to science, not withdrawn any from it"; "we are not at war"; and, of the other side, "a few disgruntled cold-war physicists". Earlier, as quoted by others: Sokal (Le Monde, 31 January 1997) reports Latour telling Libération (3 December 1996) that the hoax was "a clever joke" that thrashed people who deserved it but not researchers in science studies; Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) translate a sentence of Latour's Le Monde article of 18 January 1997 about "A small number of theoretical physicists deprived of the fat budgets of the cold war". That article was not read, and the same editors later printed an "Apology" (unread), so the wording is given only as theirs. Fuller (1998) reports that at the LSE Latour "supported" constructivism but "opposed" relativism. Later reading, not evidence for the claim: in 2004 Latour asked, "Was I wrong to participate in the invention of this field known as science studies?", while refusing "to swear that I will never be a constructivist any more".

edges.relationship: Historians of science answer the charge that their field is hostile to or ignorant of science (1996–99)
edges.evidence_note: In-period replies by historians of science, read. Steven Shapin, "Rarely Pure and Never Simple" (Configurations 7, 1999), writing as "a historian and a sociologist of science": methodological relativism "implies nothing at all about epistemological evaluations or ontological judgments" (pp. 3–4); the charge of hostility to science or ignorance of it, "—when directed to the work of many distinguished historians and sociologists of science—now deserves to be called by its proper name: it is malevolently misinformed" (p. 11). He names no protagonist; his target is identified by its arguments, such as Sokal's challenge to jump from a window. John Krige (Physics World, December 1998): Intellectual Impostures "is essentially a political tract" and "lamentably indifferent to the history and philosophy of science". Mara Beller (Physics Today 51:9, 1998): "The philosophical pronouncements of Bohr, Born, Heisenberg and Pauli deserve some of the blame for the excesses of the postmodernist critique of science." M. Norton Wise reviewed Higher Superstition in Isis (1996; unread); Edge reports his charge of "a willful strategy of distortion and demonization" (p. 323). Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997) criticised both sides and are not counted as one-way critics. Not every historian of science sided against the warriors: Margaret Jacob wrote against Latour in A House Built on Sand (1998; see the truthdebate → latour edge). Physicists also criticised historians' method (Weinberg 1996 on Whig history; Sokal and Bricmont 1998, p. 69 n. 88); that thinner charge is not drawn as a sciencewars → science edge. The arrow targets the debate as a whole: these historians answered the attackers' arguments (Gross and Levitt, Sokal, Sokal and Bricmont, Weinberg), not the respondents' strand in which they sit.

edges.relationship: Selected constructionist and relativist positions within science studies attacked (1994–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts. Jardine and Frasca-Spada (SHPS 1997, §I, read) report that Gross and Levitt went after "exponents of science studies -- that is, historians, philosophers and sociologists of science" (the book itself unread). Sokal (1997/98, read) disclaims that the hoax proves "the whole field of cultural studies, or cultural studies of science -- much less sociology of science -- is nonsense", yet attacks "the sloppy thinking and glib relativism that have become prevalent in many parts of Science Studies". The Social Text editors (Robbins and Ross, 1996, read) say science studies and cultural studies had "been subject recently to so much derision from conservatives in science". Koertge's anthology (1998; publisher abstract, not her text) addresses the view in "Science, Technology and Society Studies (STS)" that scientific results are "social constructions". An STS reply in its own words was not read: the Social Text essays (Harding, Fuller, Winner and others) are unread, and Robbins and Ross wrote as cultural-studies editors, so no sts → sciencewars edge is drawn.

edges.relationship: Physicists blame an "immoderate" Kuhn for founding relativism about science, while sparing the "moderate" Kuhn and leaving him to historians (1996–98)
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read. Sokal and Bricmont (1998; Profile 1999/2003 printing), following Tim Maudlin, separate "a moderate Kuhn and his immoderate brother": "We have no objection of principle to the moderate Kuhn, and we leave to historians the task of investigating the extent to which these ideas are correct in concrete situations. By contrast, the immoderate Kuhn - who became, perhaps involuntarily, one of the founding fathers of contemporary relativism - thinks that changes of paradigm are due principally to non-empirical factors" (p. 70). Weinberg (1996) lists Kuhn, "as I understand them", among those who deny "The objective nature of scientific knowledge"; in 1998 he wrote that Kuhn's later conclusions "have made Kuhn a hero to the philosophers, historians, sociologists, and cultural critics who question the objective character of scientific knowledge", and that "Kuhn made the shift from one paradigm to another seem more like a religious conversion than an exercise of reason." Sokal's parody (1996, n. 2) cites Kuhn (1970) first among the "revisionist studies" it mocks. This is a critique of Kuhn and of his reception; Kuhn died in 1996 and did not reply. His own earlier rejection of irrationalism ("labels which I categorically reject", 1970) is recorded on the science → kuhn edge.

edges.relationship: Appleby, Hunt and Jacob judge the strong programme's relativism inadequate to historical and scientific truth (1994)
edges.evidence_note: The historians' own words: Telling the Truth about History (1994), read in the Norton 2011 e-book, which has no print page numbers; cited by chapter. Ch. 5 ("Discovering the Clay Feet of Science"): the social constructionists "could not explain the way in which technical problems, or new natural phenomena like viruses, set whole research agendas"; the social insight "does not, however, underwrite the more extreme claims of strong programmers who have never offered an adequate theory to address the complexity of circumstances and situations that produce reasonably true human knowledge"; "relativism fails the needs of historians just as it skirts the possible existence of truths in science" (n. 24 cites Barnes and Bloor, "Relativism, Rationalism and the Sociology of Knowledge"). Ch. 7 calls social constructionists "once called strong programmers". The book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax. No SSK reply to it was found; Shapin's 1999 complaint that methodological relativism is "routinely misrepresented" (n. 6) is a general answer, not a reply to this book. Print pages remain to be checked.
edges.map_label: Telling the Truth against the strong programme, 1994

edges.relationship: Telling the Truth about History assimilates Latour's laboratory studies to postmodernism (1994); Jacob carries the objection to the Science Wars anthology (1998)
edges.evidence_note: Telling the Truth about History (1994; Norton 2011 e-book, no print pages), ch. 6 ("Postmodernism and the Crisis of Modernity"), quotes the claim that "'Nothing special'" and "'nothing extraordinary'" happens in the laboratory, attributes it in n. 9 to Latour, "Give Me a Laboratory and I Will Raise the World" (1983), and comments: "Latour calls himself an 'a-modernist,' but his position seems indistinguishable from postmodernism." Margaret Jacob, one of the three authors, then wrote "Reflections on Bruno Latour's Version of the Seventeenth Century" for A House Built on Sand (1998). Only the publisher's abstract was read; it says the essay "seeks to show how wrong-headed" We Have Never Been Modern is about early modern politics. That wording is the publisher's, not Jacob's. Moderate support: one sentence of the book, plus an abstract. No reply by Latour to these historians was found.

edges.relationship: Two 1990s disputes over relativism and truth: historians defending historical knowledge, and scientists attacking science studies
edges.evidence_note: Comparison only. The disputes overlap in time and in people but neither is a critique of the other. Margaret Jacob took part in both: Telling the Truth about History (1994) already criticised the strong programme and Latour from the historians' side, and she wrote for A House Built on Sand (1998; abstract only). Richard Evans, a truthdebate historian, cited Sokal approvingly in 1999 as having done "far more effectively and knowledgeably" what he had only touched on in criticising Derrida and Lyotard. The historians' book was published in 1994, before the 1996 hoax, and Evans endorses Sokal rather than criticising him, so no critique edge is drawn in either direction. The Science Wars concerned the natural sciences and their students; the truth debate concerned historical writing.

edges.relationship: Popper, Lakatos and the historian L. Pearce Williams criticise Kuhn's normal science and theory change: indoctrination, irrationalism, "mob psychology" and too little history (1965–70), answered by Kuhn
edges.evidence_note: In-period texts read in Lakatos and Musgrave, eds., Criticism and the Growth of Knowledge (1970; the 1965 Bedford College symposium). Popper, already a critic on the science roster: the normal scientist "has been taught in a dogmatic spirit: he is a victim of indoctrination" (p. 53); "Kuhn's logic is the logic of historical relativism" (p. 55); the Myth of the Framework "is, in our time, the central bulwark of irrationalism" (p. 56); yet "'Normal' science, in Kuhn's sense, exists" (p. 52). Lakatos, a contributor on the science roster: Kuhn's message "had some authoritarian and irrationalist overtones" (p. 92 n. 3); "in Kuhn's view scientific revolution is irrational, a matter for mob psychology" (p. 178, italicised in the original); he also absorbs Kuhn, offering his research programmes as a reconstruction of Kuhn's "socio-psychological concept of 'paradigm'" (p. 179 n. 1). L. Pearce Williams, a historian of science, aims at Kuhn and Popper alike: "the history of science cannot bear such a load at this time. We simply do not know enough to permit a philosophical structure to be erected on a historical foundation"; "As a historian, then, I must view both Popper and Kuhn with a somewhat jaundiced eye" (p. 50), while continuing to use both as guides. Kuhn's replies: charges of "irrationality, relativism, and the defence of mob rule" are "labels which I categorically reject" (p. 234); such misinterpretations "are voiced only by philosophers" (p. 260); to Pearce Williams, "There is no area in which I am more deeply conscious of the need for additional historical research, though I dissent from the conclusions Pearce Williams draws from that need" (pp. 251–252); and in the 1970 Postscript, good reasons "function as values" (p. 199) and "That is not a relativist's position" (p. 206). The irrationalism charge came from philosophers on the science roster; the historian's objection was evidential. edge_332 (science → kuhn, influence) stays.

edges.relationship: Latour and Callon: the strong programme's symmetry is itself asymmetrical, explaining nature by society, so SSK must take "one more turn" (1992–99), after an acknowledged debt
edges.evidence_note: Latour's own words, read. Debt first: in 1988 he wrote that Bloor "has most clearly defined the task of any sociology of science by introducing the notion of symmetry" and that "the principle of symmetry remains the basis of most work in the area", while dropping social explanation (Pasteurization of France, p. 256 n. 21); in 1999, "I feel entirely in David's debt" (p. 114); edge_685 records that debt. Critique: "One More Turn after the Social Turn" (1992; author's typescript, §2): "Bloor's book (1976) was the high tide mark of this asymmetrical philosophy"; "Society was supposed to explain Nature!" (p. 278 as cited by Bloor); §3: the "intermediary solution —social realism alternating with natural relativism— advocated for many years by colleagues like David Bloor or Harry Collins" is "in the long run, counterproductive for the field as well as for their own program". Callon and Latour (1992): "We have never been interested in giving a social explanation of anything, but we want to explain society" (p. 348); their yardstick lets them "read most of SSK as 'reactionary,' because they start from a closed definition of the social and then use this repertoire as an explanation of nature" (p. 349); Collins "simply shifts the burden to the Edinburgh school" (p. 355), though "We learned a great deal from Collins's work" (p. 344). We Have Never Been Modern (1993, p. 94; OCR gaps): Bloor's principle of symmetry "leads rapidly to an impasse"; "Constructivist where Nature is concerned, it is realistic about [Society]". "For David Bloor… and Beyond" (1999): "The Strong Program was useful and still is against the few remaining epistemologists. It has become an obstacle for the continuation of science studies" (p. 116). Bloor's reply: Latour's "criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects" (Anti-Latour, 1999, p. 82); see ssk → latour. Callon has no entry and sits on the sts roster.

edges.relationship: Bloor answers that Latour misrepresents the Strong Program and that his own alternative is "obscurantism" (1999); Collins and Yearley had called the actor-network approach a "backward step" (1992)
edges.evidence_note: Bloor's own words, read in "Anti-Latour" (SHPS 30, 1999): "Bruno Latour is a vehement critic of the sociology of knowledge in general, and the Strong Program in particular" (p. 81); "I think Latour is wrong ... If anything they are a step backwards" (p. 82); "his criticisms are based on a systematic misrepresentation of the position he rejects, and ... his own approach, in so far as it is different, is unworkable" (p. 82); the charge that SSK explains nature by society "is a profound misrepresentation. The aim isn't to explain nature, but to explain shared beliefs about nature" (p. 87); Latour's vocabulary of actants "looks like a formula for imposing confusion on ourselves: it is obscurantism raised to the level of a general methodological principle" (p. 97); "Latour has endorsed, and encouraged, a wholly false stereotype of the Strong Program", joining "the recent contributors to The Flight from Science and Reason" (pp. 110–111). He partly concedes: "Latour, rightly, rejects the symmetry principle understood in this way" (p. 84). He cites other critiques he finds "devastating" (p. 95), including Collins and Yearley (1992), Schaffer (1991) and Shapin (1988), none read here. Collins and Yearley's chapter is known only through Callon and Latour's quotations (1992, p. 347): "The consequences of the semiotic method [of Latour] amount to a backward step". Latour's reply acknowledges the charge: "The result is a devastating critique" (1999, p. 113) and calls Schaffer's similar critique "exactly as ill-conceived" (n. 6). Bloor's rejoinder (SHPS 30, pp. 131–136) was not located.

edges.relationship: Kuhn calls the strong programme's claims "absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad" (1991)
edges.evidence_note: Kuhn's own words, read: "The Trouble with the Historical Philosophy of Science" (Rothschild Lecture, Harvard, 19 November 1991; published 1992; in The Road Since Structure, 2000): "I am among those who have found the claims of the strong program absurd: an example of deconstruction gone mad. And the more qualified sociological and historical formulations that currently strive to replace it are, in my view, scarcely more satisfactory" (p. 110); the strong program "has been widely understood as claiming that power and interest are all there are" (p. 110). In the 1995 Athens interview (same volume) he says of Shapin and Schaffer's Leviathan and the Air-Pump, "The scholarship is often damn good!", while objecting that they "totally miss" the barometer's "vastly greater explanatory power" (pp. 316–317); that remark concerns the science roster's practice strand and is context only. No SSK reply to the lecture was read. The SSK reading of Kuhn ran the other way, as appropriation (Barnes, T. S. Kuhn and Social Science, 1982, unread); edge_132 (kuhn → ssk, influence) stays.

edges.relationship: A historian of consumption and material culture criticises actor-network theory's "flat view of modern history" while proposing to historicise its concerns (2009)
edges.evidence_note: Dated 2009. Frank Trentmann, "Materiality in the Future of History" (Journal of British Studies 48, 2009; read in full). He writes as a historian of consumption (author note: director of the Cultures of Consumption research programme, 2002–07) and sets material-culture studies against material politics (p. 285). "The most influential (if controversial) platform for exploring the 'agency' of things in the past couple of decades has been actor-network theory (ANT). Spearheaded by Bruno Latour, Michel Callon, John Law, and others" (p. 290); n. 33 notes "the difficulty of integrating historical formations of power and culture in an analysis primarily concerned with reconstructing a network of actors and actants at a specific moment in time" (p. 290). "It is perhaps ironic that a theory like ANT, so concerned with resisting grand narratives and abstractions (like 'society'), draws on such a flat view of modern history"; "It is hard to see a general turning away from things, as presumed by Latour and others" (p. 291); "this rather monochromatic view of modernity supposedly so divorced from things" (p. 301). The critique is qualified: "Before simply rejecting Latour as problematic history, however, we might historicize his concerns into questions for research" (p. 301), and whatever one thinks of the claim that things have agency, "things and humans are inseparably interwoven in mutually constitutive relationships" (p. 307). No reply by Latour was found. A historian's critique of Latour; not a claim that consumption history as a field rejected ANT.

edge_138.relationship: offers a comparison between programme-based sociological explanation and laboratory ethnography
edge_138.evidence_note: Comparative teaching link between two methods, not an assertion of a one-way genealogy or of agreement: the Strong Programme's causal and symmetrical explanation of accepted and rejected belief, and Latour and Woolgar's laboratory ethnography of how facts are made. Shared objects do not establish a simple Bloor-to-Latour lineage. The acknowledged debt is edge_685. The disagreement of 1992–99 is carried by the two critique edges of revision 1.135 (latour → ssk and ssk → latour), which hold the Bloor–Latour exchange and its sources.

rationale: An outside review (plans/2026-10-13-gemini-review-backlog.md) found that 70 of 166 entries had no critique edge, and that kuhn, latour, ssk, sts and science had none. Research of 2026-10-14 (data/extension-2026/science-studies-critique-2026-10-14/evidence-kuhn-critics.md, evidence-ssk-latour.md, evidence-science-wars.md; data/extension-2026/pathway-endpoints-2026-10-14/evidence-new-materialism.md for Trentmann) read the critics and the replies. The Science Wars attackers (Gross, Levitt, Sokal, Bricmont, Weinberg, Mermin, Koertge) have no atlas home, so only a debate entry can carry their critiques; its participants named the dispute in period (Social Text, 1996), and historians of science intervened on both sides. Edges rest on primary passages read in period texts, on quotations by in-period readers (labelled as such), on publisher abstracts (labelled), and, for Trentmann (2009) and Latour (2004), on dated later work; Higher Superstition, Wise 1996, Latour's Le Monde article and most of A House Built on Sand were not read and are cited only through in-period readers or abstracts. Thin candidates (sciencewars → science, → gender; sts → sciencewars) are not drawn. Canadian-PhD uptake is recorded as metadata only.

row.context: A historian of science at the 1965 symposium on Kuhn, sceptical of Kuhn and Popper alike: "the history of science cannot bear such a load at this time" (1970, p. 50). He kept using both as guides; Kuhn replied that he dissented "from the conclusions Pearce Williams draws".
row.works: "Normal Science, Scientific Revolutions and the History of Science" (1970)

row.context: A historian of consumption who calls for a history of materiality joining material culture to politics and practice; he questions actor-network theory's "flat view of modern history" while proposing to "historicize" Latour's concerns (2009).
row.works: "Materiality in the Future of History: Things, Practices, and Politics" (2009)
